h1: Buying homebrew ingredients online in India and checking freshness
title: Buying Homebrew Ingredients in India | Craft Beer School
desc: How to buy malt, hops and yeast online in India and check each for freshness when the parcel arrives, with what to look and smell for.
teaser: A parcel that sat in a 40 °C courier van can ruin a brew before you start. Here is what to check when it lands.
standfirst: Most Indian homebrewers buy ingredients online. The parcel often spends days in the heat. Malt, hops and yeast each go stale in a different way. Knowing the signs lets you catch a bad batch before brew day.
sections: Why freshness is harder in India

Homebrew ingredients are mostly imported. Malt comes from European or Australian maltsters, hops from the US, Europe or New Zealand, yeast from labs abroad. By the time they reach a homebrew shop in Bengaluru, Pune or Delhi, they have already travelled for weeks. Then the final courier leg adds days in vans and sorting hubs that can run well above 35 °C in summer.

Heat and humidity are the two enemies. Hops lose aroma in heat. Yeast loses viability. Malt picks up moisture in the monsoon and goes soft. None of that shows on a product page, so the checks happen when the parcel arrives.
When to order and how to ship

A few habits reduce the risk before you even open the box:

  • Order early in the week so the parcel does not sit in a hub over a weekend.
  • In summer, ask whether the seller ships liquid yeast and hops with an ice pack or insulation. Many will.
  • Order close to brew day for hops and liquid yeast, not months ahead.
  • Buy whole malt rather than crushed if you have a grain mill. Whole grain keeps for months; crushed grain is best used within a couple of weeks.

Be home for delivery if you can. A parcel left on a sunny landing for an afternoon undoes the seller's cold chain.

Hops are the most fragile ingredient. Good hop pellets come in foil packs that are vacuum sealed or flushed with nitrogen. The pack should be tight around the pellets, not puffed up or loose. A loose pack means air got in.

Look for the crop year on the label. Hops are harvested once a year, so a pack two or three crops old has probably lost much of its aroma even if it was stored well. Open one pack and check the pellets. They should be green and smell bright: citrus, pine, fruit or herbs depending on the variety. Brown pellets that smell of cheese or old socks are oxidised. That cheesy note comes from isovaleric acid, which forms as hop acids break down. Use those only for bittering, if at all.

Malt is tougher, but it still goes off. Bite a kernel of whole malt. Fresh, dry malt is crisp and crunchy and tastes sweet and bready. Malt that has taken on moisture is chewy and tastes flat or stale. Crushed malt should smell sweet, like biscuits, not musty.

Check for insects too. Small beetles or webbing in a sack mean grain pests got in somewhere along the way. Look at the bag for the maltster's details and, where printed, a packing or best-before date. Crystal and roasted malts are especially quick to soften in humid weather because they are dried to low moisture and pull water back from the air.

Dry yeast is the safest buy in India. It tolerates heat far better than liquid yeast and has a long shelf life. Check the best-before date on the sachet and that the sachet is sealed and not puffy. Store it in the fridge once it arrives.

Liquid yeast is a live culture with a shorter life. Check the manufacture or best-before date and feel the pack: it should arrive cool, not warm. Older or heat-stressed liquid yeast needs a starter, a small batch of wort that wakes the cells and grows their numbers before brew day. Our guide to first homebrew mistakes explains why underpitching is so common.

Liquid malt extract darkens and develops a twangy, stale flavour with age and heat. Check the date and favour fresh stock. Dry malt extract keeps better but clumps into a hard block if humidity gets in, so check that the bag is sealed. Priming sugar, finings and water salts are stable; just check packs are sealed and labelled.

Bottles and caps arrive more often by courier now as well. If you are buying those too, our guide to bottles and caps covers what to look for.
Store it properly the moment it arrives

All the checking in the world is wasted if the parcel then sits in a warm cupboard. Hops go straight into the freezer, still sealed. Yeast goes into the fridge. Malt goes into an airtight container away from the stove and the sun. Write the date on everything with a marker.

Keep a short note of what you received and how it looked. If a supplier keeps sending loose hop packs or old yeast, you will have the record to raise it or switch.

Your first step: next time a parcel arrives, open the hop packs and smell them before they go in the freezer. Write the crop year and date on each one.
faqs: How can I tell if hops are stale?
Fresh pellets are green and smell bright. Brown pellets or a cheesy, sweaty smell mean the hops have oxidised and lost aroma.
How long does crushed malt last?
Crushed malt is best used within a couple of weeks, sooner in humid weather. Whole malt kept dry and airtight lasts for months.
Is dry yeast better than liquid yeast in India?
For most homebrewers, yes. Dry yeast handles heat in transit much better and keeps longer. Liquid yeast needs a cold chain and often a starter.
What should I do with ingredients when they arrive?
Put hops in the freezer, yeast in the fridge and malt in an airtight container somewhere cool. Label each with the date.
